Senate Reform SUPPLY
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Fournier (Hull) for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations on the amendment moved this afternoon by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) with regard to the question of Senate reform. I do not think any serious person, certainly no serious person interested in the institutions of our country, can be happy when he surveys the position of the Senate at the present time. Even those of us on the outside, who do not participate in its proceedings and have no responsibility for it, cannot help but feel that it is a sad and indeed serious thing that an institution which has played a worthy part in the past and which in my opinion has an opportunity of playing a worthy part in the future should be allowed to languish in the position in which the Senate finds itself at the present time.
It is not as though a second chamber were a new idea that had not been tested before. We all know that second chambers have been employed by practically all serious, civilized nations in their forms of government. There may have been some changes during the war, but immediately before the war it could be said that few countries, and no major countries, were without a second chamber.
I am not going to pursue that further than to say that I think every serious person will wish, not that the Senate should be abolished but that it should be improved. Of course, Senate reform has become a kind of joke in this country because it has been talked about so long and nothing has been done about it. It has become like the weather. I want to recall to hon. members the fact that for thirty years-yes, thirty years-the matter has been commonly talked about. I go back to an incident in this house many years ago; it is not thirty years ago, but it is some twenty-six or twenty-seven years ago. I quote from Hansard of 1926-27, page 355, when the famous pledge with which nearly all members are familiar was disclosed or at any rate confirmed by the former prime minister in this house, in answer to a question by Mr. Evans. Mr. Evans asked this question:
1.	What is the form or wording of the pledge, if any, taken from those who have been appointed senators during the last two years with a view to Senate reform?
2.	How many have been thus pledged?
[Mr. Speaker.!
Here is Mr. King's answer:
1.	An assurance of support of such measure of Senate reform, in conformity with the requirements of the constitution, as may be introduced by the Liberal administration.
That is Mr. King's answer, that the formal wording of the pledge was an assurance of support. And his answer to the question, how many, is this:
2.	This assurance has been given by all who have accepted appointments to the Senate within the time mentioned.
Then two years ago the hon. member for Winnipeg Centre-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: North Centre.

I am sorry,
the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked again as to these pledges; and again the then prime minister, Mr. King, replied. He said as reported at page 854 of Hansard of 1948:
There was nothing in the nature of a written pledge. There was no pledge made to the government, as a government. It was an undertaking that was given to myself, as the one who is responsible for nominating members to the Senate. How many there were from whom I received that assurance, I cannot say at the present time. Nor am I in a position to say just when I ceased to raise that question. It did not become as important later on when we had a majority in the senate-
There a delightful confession that you should all observe. In other words, Mr. King says in effect that he lost interest in it as soon as there was a majority in the Senate.
It did not become as important later on when we had a majority in the Senate, and were, in a position to see that permanent legislation originating in this house was not defeated because of action on the part of a hostile opposition in the upper chamber.
I shall have occasion to show in a moment or two, Mr. Speaker, that there were different views held of the Senate-much better and higher views, in my opinion-and they were held by people, I am glad to say, in both of the old parties.
I call the attention of the house to this pledge situation. I do not know whether we should ask an accounting from these senators, who were appointed many years ago with the idea of Senate reform very much in their minds perhaps, and certainly in the prime minister's mind. I do not know whether to picture them as straining at the leash in all these years in order to have Senate reform effectuated. I do not know whether they were held back by the then prime minister or whether the reverse was the case; but at any rate we all know that during all these years nothing has been done except the uttering of a lot of brave words.

Then we come to the amendment this afternoon, and I should like to refer to what was said by the leader of the C.C.F. party. He said, and I think very truly, that this is a proposal we might well have expected to receive from the government. Certainly after all these years we might have expected to receive it. We did not, however, receive it from the government. What is worse than that, apparently not only was it not to be done by the government but it was not to be done by anybody else because apparently in this house only the government can initiate things. When this moderate resolution was initiated this afternoon by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) took the view that nothing should be suggested from this side of the house because he said that by so doing the leader of the opposition was inviting the house to defeat the government, to which the leader of the opposition quite properly replied that he was doing nothing of the kind, and that we should be only too delighted if the government saw fit to accept this motion and to vote for it.
I should be fair to the Prime Minister, or try to be. The other afternoon I made this same complaint that nothing could be accepted from this side of the house-it was in discussing a rather minor measure-and I must say that the Prime Minister behaved handsomely. He took me up on it. He said no, that was not the case; and in fact my amendment was accepted. It was a rather small matter, and it seems to me perfectly clear now that that was just a momentary relaxation of the rule that nothing at all must come from this side of the house, that nothing must originate except on the other side, and anything from here must be promptly voted down.
I must say that I think the Prime Minister enjoys greatly having a large majority, and I have no doubt that we all would. It is pleasant to see him look around the house and survey the serried ranks; and this afternoon he issued a kind of trumpet call at the end of his speech, saying that he hoped all those who supported him would vote with him. Really, that seemed to me to be a pure waste of words because there is little indication that there will ever be any doubt on that question.
But the Prime Minister gave another reason for refusing to accept this amendment this afternoon; and that reason was, if I may say so with proper deference to the Prime Minister, a most preposterous reason. As to accepting this amendment which suggests that the question of Senate reform might be presented to the government for discussion at the. forthcoming dominion-provincial constitutional conference, the Prime
Senate Reform
Minister took an extremely high line and said that to do that would be to break faith with the provinces. I was a little bit startled when he used the words "break faith" because the Prime Minister on the whole uses words accurately, and breaking faith is not a charge that one likes to level hastily and carelessly at anybody. As I say, I was startled when I read the moderate wording of this resolution, but I was much more than startled-I was completely flabbergasted- when I examined the documents and found out that the Prime Minister was wholly and absolutely wrong in his suggestion, and that it was far from being a matter of breaking of faith. Incidentally I should say that I think the Prime Minister realized later on that to say it was a matter of breaking faith was going a bit far and he used different language; he said something to the effect that it would not be quite within the spirit of the negotiations which had taken place between the dominion and the provinces.
Let us have a look at that. Let me first of all read a short extract from an article written some little time since, but since last January, by Senator Lambert, which article begins with these words:
During the dominion-provincial constitutional conference held in Ottawa last January, particular reference was made to the Senate by Hon. Angus L. Macdonald of Nova Scotia.
He said that the sections in the B.N.A. Act dealing with the Senate were "of importance to the provinces no less than to the dominion." He contended that before any change in those sections could be effected, the consent of seven provinces out of ten would be essential to any proposed amendments by the dominion.
And I read on:
The agenda for the meeting of the official representatives of the dominion and the provinces next autumn to discuss further ways and means of amending the B.N.A. Act should certainly contain an item relating to Senate reform.
And reading further on, he says:
That is why the recent remarks of Hon. Wishart Robertson, the government leader in the Senate... have been attracting some attention throughout the country.
And again he says:
In his reply now recorded in Hansard, and widely reported at the time in the Canadian press, Senator Robertson said that he was not interested so much in the headlines of the newspapers as he was in the effective performance of the duties of the Senate.
But do not let me rely wholly on an article written by Senator Lambert, although he is a responsible person and, I understand, is not many miles removed from the confidence of the Liberal high command. Let me read an extract from a speech made by Mr. St. Laurent himself last January at the conference, from which I read briefly as follows.

Senate Reform
In answer to a question by Mr. Macdonald of Nova Scotia, at page 76 he is reported as follows:
The field really narrows down to these matters whicn afiiect the set-up of the central authority.
Then I skip a little bit and go on:
For instance, those which refer to the Senate and to the representation in the House of Commons are, I think, a part of the Canadian constitution.
And more clearly, he says at page 94:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Would it be fair to take it, as
a result of our deliberations, that there is no objection raised to entrenching . . .
Then I skip through three or four lines and he says:
... a provision that the representation of the people of a province in the House of Commons would not fall below its representation in the Senate.
In other words, the question of Senate reform was discussed then; and to suggest that that is in some way improper is, I think, so far from the mark that I am amazed at the Prime Minister for ever slipping into such an error.
I will now take just a moment or two to refer to a conception of the duties of the Senate and to the usefulness and possibilities of the Senate which were held in that chamber not so very many years ago, and expressed first of all by Senator Raoul Dandurand who was at one time leader of the Senate in the 1920's, and also some remarks of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen who was leader of the Senate from 1930 to 1935.
I would ask hon. members first of all to note the unanimity of opinion between these two men as to the duties, responsibilities and possibilities of the Senate. Second, I would ask them to note the high and useful conception which they had of the position of the Senate; and further, before I sit down I want to point out that that is not merely an imaginary picture of what should be, but a picture of what has been when the Senate has been properly conducted.
First of all, I shall read from an article in the Queen's university Quarterly. That is a publication which should be much more widely read than it is. Perhaps I may take advantage of this occasion to put in a plug for it. I am reading from page 21 of the issue of the spring of 1950:
In 1922, soon after becoming government leader of the Senate, the late Senator Raoul Dandurand addressed his colleagues on the manner in which, he thought, the Senate should function. Analysing the character and work of the Senate he called for a return to the position of the first sessions of that body when Senators acted like "independent judges". He added, "For my part, I refuse to lead a ministerial party in this chamber; I claim no followers; I shun party discipline and the party
rMr. Macdonnell (Greenwood).]
whip." Later in his career, after the Conservative party victory in 1930, he became leader of the opposition in the Senate. On this occasion he recurred to his statement of 1922 and deprecated the reference to himself by any such title as "leader of the opposition", with its implication of partisanship.
The article goes on:
Similar views have been expressed from time to time by other distinguished Senators. Senator Arthur Meighen, for years the Conservative party leader in the Senate, contributed a brilliant article to Queen's Quarterly in the summer of 1937. In it he emphasized the unique position of the Senate in the Canadian governmental scheme, and declared that the Senate's fundamental basis was that of representing territory as "against arbitrary action of a bare majority" possible in the House of Commons. He pointed out the Senate's supreme obligation to protect racial, political and economic minorities. Like Dandurand, he asserted that the forms of partisanship should be submerged.
And so on. Before I take my seat, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read another extract from the article by Mr. Meighen, because I suggest again that it puts before us in the clearest language the usefulness, the objective which should be before the Senate, and which distinguishes it sharply from this house. He said:
The Senate is worthless if it becomes merely another Commons divided upon party lines and indulging in party debates such as are familiar in the lower chamber session after session. If the Senate ever permits itself to fulfil that function and that alone in the scheme of confederation, then the sooner it is abolished the better. This practice is not to be deprecated in the House of Commons. If we are going to have a democracy, the practice must continue. There have to be parties and party manoeuvres; there have to be conflicts and controversies innumerable in variety and wearisome in length.
Mr. Meighen could speak with some experience about that. I continue:
The great scheme of bringing sections together, letting each see the viewpoint of the other, has to be worked out in the representative chamber. Sometimes we are too impatient and critical of governments in allowing what seems inordinate time for discussion of public business. That discussion is good, but it is not the function of the Senate. Members of the second chamber must get away, lift their minds far from those hard-drawn lines of party, or they cannot serve their country. They have to make up their minds to give every government fair play and not to stand in the way of legislation unless they are convinced it must be defeated on its merits, and that the consequences of failure to defeat it would be serious; nor to stand stubbornly in the path of any government proposal unless it is brought there in their judgment to serve the ends of party by largess in this or some other part of the dominion rather than the true interests cf the nation.
I have no intention of detaining the house longer. I have put before the house these opinions expressed by men who served their country well. Before I take my seat I should like to remind the house-and I hope I do not say this in any partisan sense because it was possible only because both sides

worked at it-of the relationship between this chamber and the Senate in the years 1930 to 1935. Anyone who takes the trouble to look into the matter will find that first of all the Senate was left absolutely free by the then prime minister, Mr. Bennett. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that the reputation of that great man will live when the reputation of many of the detractors who are so fond of picking out little things will not even be a memory of a memory. But anyone who will take the trouble to find out what went on in the Senate between 1930 and 1935 will be convinced that I am right. That was not wholly due to Lord Bennett and Mr. Meighen. It was partly because Senator Dandurand took the same view as I have read here tonight. It was partly also because of course there was much more of equality in numbers in the Senate at that time.
To me there is nothing sadder than to see this body of able men-and there are many able men in the Senate-reduced to the point where in public estimation its reputation I suppose was never so low. That seems to me to be a crying shame. I was glad to hear the leader of the C.C.F. party refer to the obligation of the government. It seems to me a shame that this thing is to be stood over again. It is being stood over for reasons that in my opinion are utterly insubstantial, and the opportunity of doing something to rescue this great institution, before it falls too low, before public opinion reaches the point where it demands that it be done away. with to the great injury of us all, may be lost.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to support the principle of the amendment moved this afternoon by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). There are some points of detail in connection with this motion to which I might take exception, but I agree with its spirit and principle, and if it comes to a vote, I shall vote for it.
One of the reasons that I support this motion is that I feel a committee which had an opportunity to discuss the place of the Senate in our parliamentary set-up in this latter part of the twentieth century would have a chance to consider the desirability of abolishing the Senate altogether. In my view that is the most desirable and most useful means of reform, and I believe it to be in keeping with the thinking and the wishes of the Canadian people-certainly where I come from.
I am going to come back in a few moments to my argument that the Senate should be
Senate Reform
abolished, but before I do there are two things that I want to say. First I want to say this very clearly. In the minds of all of us, I am sure, there is a clear-cut distinction between the men and women who occupy places in the Senate and the Senate as an institution. As a matter of fact I feel sorry for the hon. gentlemen and ladies in the other place, that they have to take the kind of criticism that is offered; I hope they realize that it is criticism of the institution and not of themselves as individuals. I was counting up some days ago, and I believe there are about eighteen members in the Senate at the present time who were members of the House of Commons when I first came here eight years ago. In other words they are persons whom I got to know fairly well, and for whom I have a high regard. The same is true for others who were there before I came here and whom I have met in other ways.
So I wish to make it clear that, for my part-and I am sure all hon. members feel this way-when I criticize the Senate as an institution and when I voice feelings of disrespect and even ridicule felt by people in Canada, it casts no reflection upon the individuals of the Senate themselves.
Another thing I wish to do just now is to deal with two of the points at any rate-there might have been a third, but I did not make a note of it-raised by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) this afternoon in his objection to this amendment. In the first place he objected to it on the ground that it was a gilded pill. His argument was that no matter how one might dress it up, an amendment to a motion to go into committee of supply was a motion of non-confidence, which had as its purpose-perhaps, he said, its fundamental purpose-the defeat of the government.
I wish to remind the Prime Minister that at least once within the memories of many of us in the house we had an occasion when an amendment to a motion to go into supply was carried by the house, the carrying of which did not involve the defeat of the government. That happened on August 27, 1948, in connection with an amendment related to the subsidy on milk. Hon. members from all sides of the house spoke in support of the amendment, whereupon the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) rose in his place and said that, so far as the government was concerned, they were willing that a free vote be taken. After that a vote was taken and the amendment carried; but the Minister of Trade and Commerce then got to his feet and, relying upon citation 489 in Beauchesne's second edition, again moved that Mr. Speaker leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply.

Senate Reform
The whole procedure was perfectly in order. The life of the government was not at stake at all. On the other hand the house did express itself with regard to a principle. The same can happen with respect to this motion today. All the government needs to do is to say that this is a principle concerning which they would like to have an expression of the views of the house. The motion could carry and then a minister could rise immediately and, relying on the citation to which I have referred, could move again that we go into committee of supply.
I think that precedent must not be forgotten, because it is a very clear one. In view of the fact that this is one of the very few ways in which the opposition can call upon the house to vote in respect of ideas or principles which we feel should be considered, I think the government should refrain from this constant referring to it as a case of non-confidence, and simply calling upon its supporters to vote it down on that basis, without any consideration of the merits of the proposal.
The other argument the Prime Minister advanced this afternoon was that to pass a motion such as this to set up a committee to discuss Senate reform, before the dominion-provincial conference holds its further meetings, would be a case of breaking faith with the provincial governments. I wish to point out first of all that the Prime Minister himself in reading from the relevant documents this afternoon indicated that what that conference is dealing with is methods of amending the constitution, not with subject matter. This has nothing to do with the methods of amending the constitution. Rather, this is a subject matter which some of us in the house feel should be considered.
May I also point out to the Prime Minister that no less a person than the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) on March 10 of this year took the very opposite position to that taken this afternoon by the Prime Minister. That was the occasion when the Minister of National Health and Welfare was asking the house to set up a committee on old age security, upon which occasion he said, as reported at page 643 of Hansard:
As we approach these discussions with the provinces, it will be helpful for us to have the considered views of all the parties in this house, of organized labour, of industry, of representative social welfare organizations, and of other interested groups in our population, who have given study through the years to the important question of old age security. I believe that in the formulation of a policy nothing could be more desirable before we finally meet the provinces, than to take the organized labour groups of this country into our confidence through this committee, as well as the farmers and other organizations.
I think that attitude and that approach will commend itself to all hon. members.

Surely there is a difference in the kind of conference to which I was there directing attention, and the kind of conference to which the Prime Minister was referring. The conference to which he referred is one in which constitutional questions are involved. That to which I referred was a question involving financial considerations in which the jurisdictions of both federal and provincial governments were involved. I submit that, upon reconsideration, my hon. friend will realize that there is no analogy between the two situations at all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I wonder who is trying to do the gilding now. After all, the situations are exactly analogous in this respect, that in both cases we have matters of joint concern to the dominion and the provinces. In the one case the Minister of National Health and Welfare says, "Before we meet the provinces it would be a good idea to have a committee so that the government will know the views of parliament." Meantime provincial governments are no doubt getting the views of their legislatures on the question.
Similarly, in respect of ways of amending the constitution, I can imagine that many provincial governments are getting the views of their provincial legislatures on these constitutional matters before they meet the dominion government in a further session of the dominion-provincial conference.
I think that after all the government has some responsibility to parliament. It should know what parliament thinks about issues of this kind before it meets the provinces, just as the Minister of National Health and Welfare put it in connection with old age security. And even if the minister had not laid down the principle as well as he did, I suggest the idea would commend itself to hon. members that there is merit in the federal government getting the views of parliament before it meets the provinces, rather than waiting until after the die has been cast.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I would remind the hon.
member of the inconsistency of the position he now takes. On that occasion he opposed the setting up of a committee, but now he is in favour of setting one up.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I opposed the setting up of a committee, but I did not oppose parliament's discussing and taking action on the question of old age security; in fact I urged that that be done without the delay involved in holding sessions of a committee. On the other hand, what the Prime Minister is trying to do now is to prevent parliament's discussing, in whatever way it may choose, this question of

Senate reform, on the ground that that would be breaking faith with the provinces. I suggest the Minister of National Health and Welfare should have made his interjections when the Prime Minister was speaking, and should have set him on the right track.
To get around to the substance of the amendment by the leader of the opposition, I said at the outset that I believe the reform of the Senate most needed is its abolition altogether. I feel that the idea of a second chamber came out of a period in the forward development of the democratic idea, when people believed in democracy and believed in their elected representatives speaking for them, but were not quite sure and were not quite prepared to go all the way.
So, carrying over the idea that was in existence in the United Kingdom with respect to a House of Lords, which was made up of persons not elected by the people, the fathers of confederation agreed to have its counterpart here in Canada, namely, the Senate, which would be appointed rather than elected by the people.
In my view our thinking as to the validity of the democratic way has moved on considerably since 1867, and it is time now that the whole of our parliamentary set-up was on an elected basis, so that everyone in parliament would be directly responsible to the people.
That may suggest to some that the thing to do with the Senate is simply to put it on an elected rather than an appointed basis. If you do that, what you have done is to provide, shall I say, two Houses of Commons to discuss the same legislation. It seems to me that you would have a duplication of effort that would be completely unnecessary. I want to say again that so far as I am concerned anything that I say casts no reflection on the persons in the Senate. I do not even deny the fact that many of them deserve something from this country for the services they have rendered in public life. I would say that many of them probably deserve a pension of some kind for the services they have rendered in various ways, but that has nothing to do with the institution in which they are now functioning.
It is sometimes argued that it is desirable to have a second house to provide a check on hasty legislation passed in the one house. Experience has shown clearly that not since the early twenties has there been any tendency at all on the part of the other place to impose any check on the House of Commons. They are not performing that function at all. As a matter of fact things in this parliament have got to the place where what we are concerned about is not this House of Commons
55946-1761	: |
Senate Reform
being checked by the Senate but the government being responsible to this House of Commons. That is the checking job that is on our hands in this generation, maintaining the concept of responsible government.
We are getting to the place where the government thinks that once it is elected at the polls it has a free hand to carry on as it wishes until the next election. It has been said a number of times on the floor of this house that the government is responsible directly to the people. Actually the government is responsible to parliament, and primarily responsible to that section of parliament elected by the people. That is the job we should be applying ourselves to. Any notion that the Senate provides any check has been ruled out, and our job is to make sure that we in this House of Commons provide the necessary check on the government, and that is a task for members of all parties in this house.
Any suggestion that the Senate provides protection for minorities, racial, religious, provincial or regional, is gone completely when the Senate is made up of an overwhelming majority on one political side as is the case at the present time. The best way to get a voice to speak for any particular group that feels it is a minority, that feels that its voice should be heard, is to have that voice raised in this House of Commons where members know they have the authority of being elected and can therefore speak more freely and more forcibly than is the case in the other place. I know that some of those hon. gentlemen over there whom we know and to whom we sometimes talk feel that way about it; they know that they have no authority to speak on behalf of the people such as we have simply because they have not been elected.
It seems to me that these things should be very thoroughly considered. I have made my position clear, that I think that times have changed and the point has been reached where we no longer need a second chamber. That is one of the things that a committee of this kind could discuss, namely the abolition of the Senate altogether. If that committee did not agree with me and did not go all the way I would go, a discussion of these mat-' ters would produce at least some measure of reform. It is clear from the experience that all of us have had in this House of Commons that it is difficult for any member of the opposition, indeed for any private member on either side of the house, to introduce any proposition substantive in character and get it put through this House of Commons. The best he can do is to get it considered by a committee.
If anyone moved a motion for a specific brand of Senate reform, if anyone moved a

Senate Reform
motion for the abolition of the Senate, it would stand no chance of being passed. Government members would get up and say that we could not discuss such a proposition on the spur of the moment because it was the sort of thing that should be considered in committee. Here is a chance to refer this whole question, and an important one it is, to a committee to have it gone into thoroughly.
I was interested in some of the quotations that were read during the debate this afternoon by those who spoke and again this evening by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), indicating the way in which this whole question has been tossed about across the years. One of the reasons why the Senate is the butt of so much critical comment is that Senate reform has been toyed with the way it is. It is now nearly thirty years since Mr. King was a young crusader for Senate reform, both in this house and out on the hustings. I have in my hand Hansard of July 19, 1924, where Mr. King is reported on page 4872 as having said:
Mr. Speaker, having in mind the action of the second chamber with respect to the measure which has just been amended and also the fate of a number of bills adopted by the Commons and defeated in the Senate. I think hon. members will agree with me that the time has come when the Commons in Canada should seek to gain rights and privileges with respect to legislation originating in this chamber similar to those which have been obtained by the House of Commons in the parliament at Westminster. I may say that the government had under consideration, prior to the opening of this session, legislation with this end in view, but we were anxious the public should feel fully convinced of the necessity before pressing it on the attention of parliament. Hon. members will recall that at the close of the last session, and at the close of the preceding session, bills which were passed by this house and which touched matters that are very vital to the electorate failed of enactment owing to the action of the Senate. This year we have instances of bills that have passed this house in three separate sessions of parliament, and which have been rejected each time by the second chamber. I think we owe it to the people of our country with respect to laws demanded by the electorate to see to the supremacy in parliament of the elective chamber. I desire to assure the house that when parliament re-assembles steps will be taken by the government to obtain, if possible, means whereby bills may be enacted by and with the advice and consent of the House of Commons under conditions similar in principle to those which have been sanctioned for the parliament of the United Kingdom.
No one would seek to suggest what was in Mr. King's mind, but I imagine that he had in mind that at least we could get away from the situation where the Senate has a permanent veto which it can exercise year in and year out, ad infinitum, over legislation of the House of Commons, and get to the position they had at Westminster where the House of Lords could do it only so many times-the number having been reduced from time to time since then. But even that measure

of reform, if that is what Mr. King had in mind away back in the early twenties, is still not implemented in this country.
The hon. member for Greenwood had something to say about the pledges that were taken by Mr. King from those that he put into the Senate back in those years. I should like to quote what I think is an interesting excerpt from Hansard of January 12, 1926, page 105. The speaker on that occasion was Mr. C. W. Bell, who was listed as the member for West Hamilton. He said:
Not only the members of this house but the country will remember that the Prime Minister-
The reference there was to Mr. King.
-in the last three and a half years has always declared his intention of effecting great reforms for the purpose of remedying the various ills from which this dominion has been suffering. But he has consistently given, as two great obstacles to this objective, the obstruction of the Senate and the influence of the Progressive party.
The party which he later absorbed.
He made the statement from many a platform that upon his return to parliament one of the first things he would undertake would be Senate reform of such character that the upper house would be no longer in a position to render legislation futile. And speaking in London-
That was at London, Ontario, on October 16, 1925.
-on October 16 last he made a statement which, if it is not known to every member of the house and to every man and woman in the country, ought certainly to be very well known. In the hockey arena in that city on the date I mentioned he said:
''Only a few days ago a number of Senators were appointed. Every one has given me his pledged word he will be prepared, once a measure passes the Commons, to give it his support. Subsequent Senators will be appointed with that understanding, and as Providence takes away a few of the older members, you will have a Senate pledged to bring about the reforms for which the administration stands."
Well, Providence has done its part since that date but the Liberal party has not kept pace. A little later the questions, to which the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) referred, were asked. I would ask the indulgence of the house to refer to them again. These were questions by Mr. Evans and they appear in Hansard for February 16, 1927, at page 355. Let me read them:

1. What is the form or wording of
the pledge, if any, taken from those who have been appointed senators during the last two years with a view to Senate reform?
2. How many have been thus pledged?

1. An assurance of support of such measure of Senate reform, in conformity with the requirements of the constitution, as may be introduced by the Liberal administration.
2. This assurance has been given by all who have accepted appointment to the Senate within the time mentioned.

As the hon. member for Greenwood indicated, in 1948, I placed on the order paper questions similar to those asked by Mr. Evans away back in 1927, but I was unable to get as specific an answer as the then prime minister, Mr. King, had given on that occasion. He did indicate that he recalled having obtained pledges of Senate reform in those years from every member he appointed but he could not quite remember just when he discontinued the practice.
So far as Mr. King is concerned, it is pretty clear that his crusading spirit for Senate reform vanished as the number of Liberals in the Senate increased. I hope that the overpowering number of Liberals that the present government has in the other place will not prevent the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) from taking up the crusade for at least a measure of Senate reform if he cannot go all the way with me for its abolition. Here is another example of how this matter has been toyed with from time to time. On June 4, 1926, as found in Hansard of that year at page 4030, there appears this excerpt:
On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Arthur Meighen (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister if there is to be any action taken this session with respect to Senate reform? If not, when is the next move to be made in this direction and of what character?
At the next sitting of the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King (Prime Minister) :
speechtext:
I might say to my right hon. friend that the government would not like to prolong the session unduly in introducing the subject of Senate reform at this stage. My right hon. friend may be sure it will come up in due course.
In June, 1926, Mr. King did not want to prolong the session unduly to deal with Senate reform. It was to be dealt with in due course. Mr. King's period as prime minister has gone and Senate reform still remains to be carried through. The rest of the quotation is as follows:

I should like to know further, if
it is the intention of the government to call a provincial conference on the subject this summer.

I will not say just when
but no doubt a conference will be held.
Before another session?

I would not say as to that.
Any who were here in the days of Mr. King will recognize the authenticity of the remarks that I have quoted. My whole point in reading these few excerpts is to indicate the way in which the question of Senate reform has been toyed with down through the years. I think as a matter of fact that members of the Senate could get up from time to time-in that other place- on a question of privilege and complain about the way in which this whole question has been played with. They have it coming
Senate Reform
to them that the matter be taken seriously, and even though I may go further than the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has indicated in his amendment, I certainly think that the house should go at least that far, should appoint this committee and have the matter investigated. I think we owe it to ourselves, to the Canadian people, and as I have already said, to the senators themselves.
Let me conclude by reading one other quotation. When I have read it I think there will be really nothing more to say. It is taken from Hansard of January 22, 1935, at page 102. I will indicate later who the speaker was. I would rather read the quotation first. It reads:
I believe it was the leader of the opposition who raised the discussion concerning the Senate. I am making reference to all these points because I believe one would do better to put his finger on the spot where the sand may be put into the machinery.
I hear someone saying that he already knows who it is.
The right hon. gentleman has said that we have a Tory Senate. If I gather anything from the temper of the Canadian people, and if it is the policy of the Senate to put sand into the machinery, then we will have to reform the Senate. The time has long since passed when the Senate should be used as unemployment insurance for many of those in political life.
The speaker on that occasion has had something to do with unemployment insurance since then, for he was none other than the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). I suggest that we may not always agree with him now in some of the things he says, but certainly the statement that he made over in this corner of the house some fifteen years ago is very much to the point. If I may say so again, Mr. Speaker, I think it is unfair to the ladies and gentlemen in that other place as persons, that cracks like these can be made about them, that the Senate can be referred to as a scheme of unemployment insurance for some of those in political life. People who have served this country in public life for many years have some consideration coming to them, and I would say not just in the form of material assistance or pensions. They have coming to them the right to continue to serve the country in useful positions but let us not do the derogatory thing we are doing to them at the present time by simply putting them into an institution for which the country has, as the hon. member for Greenwood said, perhaps less respect now than has ever been the case.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say again that for my part I think the time has come in the development of our democratic institutions when there should be no portion of parliament that is not responsible to the electorate directly. Therefore I think we do not need

Senate Reform
the Senate at all. It should be abolished. But surely we cannot do less than to take the course that has been suggested by the leader of the opposition in his amendment, pass it, have this committee set up and get to work discussing this important question, and not leave it for another twenty-five or thirty years as has been the case already. As I sit down I remind the government that to pass the amendment does not defeat the government; that will come in due course. It would mean the setting up of the proposed committee but it would also mean, on the basis of citation 489, that the government could immediately move that we go again into committee of supply.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, an institution should continue to exist as long as it serves a useful purpose. It may be that some hon. members, like the One who has just resumed his seat, would be in favour of abolishing the Senate sooner or later, but they have not dared to say so openly. Ever since I became a member I have noticed that the matter of Senate reform has been mentioned quite often in debates in this chamber as well as outside the house. Some of those debates have shed some degree of light on this question which always attracts considerable attention.
In rising to take part in this debate, I have no intention of striking a fatal blow to the motion moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). However, as regards the upper house, where French-speaking members have so often distinguished themselves, I feel duty bound if not to rise to its defence at least to bring forth some arguments in favour of its existence, of its survival.
Since I both think and act democratically, I believe that the Senate, though its members, unlike those of the House of Commons, do not have to stand for election, nevertheless keeps an open, attentive and practised eye on the various problems considered in this house. Even though some senators are no longer young, we must recognize that they have indeed acquired some experience. That, in my opinion, counts for a great deal in a man's life. May I refer to a few words spoken by a great American industrialist, Henry Ford, who said something to this effect:
The best salary I have ever received is experience and I believe it is the most commendable thing in the world. It is something no one can take away from me.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that when a mem-Der has spent fifteen or twenty years in this house as democratic representative of a constituency of his province, of his country, he

has acquired some experience, a way of seeing things. He can also much better understand the economic, political, social and even religious problems which are fairly often brought to our attention. Too often, we hear the time-worn argument that the Senate is a body made up of people with one foot in the grave. Even if some senators are elderly, they nevertheless retain that alertness of mind that is found in younger persons. Besides, we must remember that certain members of the upper house, such as Senators Dandurand, Meighen and Beland, who had reached an advanced age, have made a very useful and commendable contribution not only to the Canadian nation but to the House of Commons.
If hon. members made it a point of finding out what goes on in the other place, they would see that during every session a great many issues are discussed in the various Senate committees, which proves the great usefulness of that hon. chamber and serves to justify its existence. The discussions that take place in those committees are important and useful enough to establish the necessity of the Senate's existence, even if its members are not elected.
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying a moment ago, a member of parliament who, for fifteen or twenty years has been a representative of the people, acquires a certain experience. I do not intend to pose as the Senate's defender, but if I put forward my views concerning it, it is not because I feel myself growing old, since after twenty-three years I am still full of the will and desire to fight. I believe that very often derogatory remarks are made concerning the other place. This subject should be approached, however, by really facing up to the problem.
There is no doubt that the point at issue is whether the Senate is useful and whether there is any justification for its existence. To prove it, we have but to listen to the proceedings of a committee of the other place on the rights and privileges of the human being. We would then see how exhaustively a matter which will eventually be submitted to this house is being discussed.
As far as that question of human rights is concerned-and it has been discussed even in the United Nations-I have followed with much interest and attention the work of the Senate committee. We can, I believe, hope that these deliberations will be of some use to us and that we will eventually benefit from them.
Besides, in every human being there is a phenomenon of a psychological nature that

makes him perfectible. As the Senate is itself made up of human beings, it is also perfectible, and even though some of its members are old, they are not less intelligent for it. If the situation need be improved in so far as the Senate is concerned, I believe that this house should undertake a more thorough discussion of this question.
The motion of the hon. leader of the opposition, in the terms in which it has been actually moved, might have the merit of initiating such discussion, but it should not be carried by this house. I go on record as opposing the resolution, not only to answer the bid of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who has urged us to oppose it, but also as a member of the Liberal party, which leaves us with our freedom of action and allows us to express our mind openly. I am of opinion that the motion is a little too premature and should be given the six months' hoist. We must all be confident that the Senate will continue to fulfil its basic function and prove its usefulness.
I have here a letter signed by Mr. Paul de Martigny, published in La Patrie. It concerns the Senate indirectly. It is about people who are pensioned off. Many members and many Canadian taxpayers want an age limit for senators. Let them listen carefully to what I am about to read and they will see that such a request is interesting for those who are not so old, but not such a good thing for those who have reached a certain age. I quote:
A man who is being retired is not very cheerful the day he bids his fellow workers farewell. Why? If you want to know, read what someone wrote to me.
Retirement means the end of the struggle for a living and brings the assurance that one will not be left in need. That is much better than being let out on the street. It also means, however, that one is retired from active life and put with the has-beens. After having counted as something for a long time, one becomes nothing. For forty years, half a century, if you like, someone has been a cog in the big machinery of society. Then, on the grounds that this cog is old, it is put aside. Not very pleasant for the party concerned.
I know, of course, that there is the other side of the picture: freedom after the long enslavement of work under conditions that sometimes proved very difficult. It is the end of each day's stupendous effort. But once the task is done, does the memory of it rankle the next day? Of course not, because people realize that life itself is made up of such little hardships which are as old as time. As we advance in years our eyes are opened, our illusions vanish, and we finally understand that life, seen at close hand, is not always beautiful.
At any rate, it is not as beautiful as the long-anticipated retirement which gradually comes closer and closer until one day it is at hand and it does not look so promising as before. Above all there is the
Senate Reform
realization that tomorrow we may no longer be of any use. Retirement is like the beginning of a long unending regret.
The more fortunate is not the retired man, it is the one who is not yet retired. It is the fellow worker struck by death at his work, like a soldier in the thick of the battle, weapons in hand.
What good is it to drag out the monotonous and useless life of the retired man?
What good is it to hark back to the same old stores of a past for which nobody cares? That is. why the wise thinks twice before he asks for his retirement. To quit the daily task, however great the effort required, is like getting away from reality, so meagre, so hard though it may be. It is acting like the dog of the good man Lafontaine, who left its prey for a shadow.
Mr. Speaker, it is another psychological phenomenon when a man has worked hard all his life for society he finds one day that he has no longer any soul, that his services are no longer required, that he is considered 'too old to take .part in public affairs.
We only need to look around us, not only in Canada but throughout the world, to see men over seventy who are still very active and who can bring into the discussion of public affairs the contribution of a valuable experience.
I need only mention the former prime minister of Great Britain, the Right. Hon. Winston Churchill, who, despite his seventy-five years, displays an extraordinarily keen mind during the Commons debates and the British elections. Thus the argument that the Senate is made up of men who are too old is worthless.
Besides, I believe the amendment was moved for the sole purpose of launching some sort of a debate and finding out the members' views on the matter.
I do not make these remarks because I have an eye on the other place, or because I want to defend the members of the Senate. I just want to say that the Senate is still a democratic institution, although its members are not elected.
Moreover, I think that the Senate should be protected against the idea, which is becoming generalized, that senators should be elected. To my mind, the Senate is endowed with a certain freedom of action which the elected representatives of the people do not enjoy.
As members of parliament we retain our liberty, but we know that we must sometimes follow public opinion instead of leading it. I remember that when I was still a student at the seminary, a former Quebec premier

Dominion-Provincial Conference told me that men in public life should lead public opinion and not follow it.
I believe that the members of the Senate are in a better position to lead public opinion under the present system than they would be if they were elected.
To those who look to the Senate with some emotion, I shall quote a proverb which I found somewhere and which speaks volumes in this respect:
The hardest thing to do is not to reach the top of the ladder, but to make one's way through the crowd at the bottom.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Fournier (Hull) for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew.

Mr. Speaker, there are a few observations that I should like to make on the amendment that is now before the house. I listened to the mover of the amendment, and I may say that I enjoyed the address he read to the house this afternoon. In fact, I had read much of the substance in it previously in Maclean's magazine, Saturday Night and other magazines, and I enjoyed it at that time. I may say that I agree with many of the things that were said.
As to reform of the Senate, I think possibly that is essential for the reason that among the people of Canada there is a strong feeling that the Senate is not filling the bill; that is, that it is not giving service commensurate with the money that is spent on it. When we speak of that matter, I think possibly we should take a look around home first of all and clean up our own backyard; because when it comes to the matter of money being spent for loafing, and days being spent in doing nothing, we have a good deal of it right here.
Senate Reform
I agree with many of the things that have been said about the matter, but I cannot agree with the amendment because of the way in which it comes before the house. If that amendment had come in as a private motion, it would then have given to hon. members supporting the government an opportunity to vote for it. It may be said that they can support it anyway. But I do not think that any of the people who elected me on June 27, including many who are Conservatives, expect me to get up and support an amendment when by doing so it amounts to a vote of non-confidence in the government which I support. I think the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), who moved the motion, will agree that we do not intend to do that and that it is not the right thing for us to do; and I at least give the hon. member who seconded the motion, the member for Lake Centre, credit for having intelligence enough not to expect us to do this. For that reason, I am not going to discuss the amendment much longer. I think that possibly a committee to study this matter would be a good thing. Many things might be done. We might give them more to do. We could possibly have a limit on the age of the senators and they would have a purpose which they could fulfil, in examining the things that go on in this house. For instance, they could examine estimates, and so on, and it would not be necessary to set up royal commissions; they could do this if necessary. I listened with interest to the speech of the leader of the C.C.F. party and also to the other hon. members of that party. I have listened to their policies along these lines for many years. I heard the same speeches about ten years ago. I will not say whether I agree with them or not. Possibly there may be something in doing away with the Senate. For the last few years I have not heard these same statements from many members of the C.C.F. party because I believe when they got into power in Saskatchewan and they were gaining ground here they thought they might be able to use the Senate. Now that they will never have a chance to get into power here they are not interested in having a Senate at all.
As I say, I agree with some of the arguments that we should have a committee to investigate this matter, but I do not think that even the mover and the seconder of the amendment would expect the government supporters to be stupid enough to vote against the government's motion.

Mr. Speaker, I am against doing away with the Senate of Canada. I am in favour of any reform that can be made in the Senate which
2788

Senate Reform
will be for the public good and for the government of this country. It does seem to me that the great cry that went up against the Senate in years gone by was on occasions when the Senate and the House of Commons were of a different political complexion.
My memory takes me back to 1897 or 1898 * when the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier passed an act in this house for the construction of a railway into the Yukon Territory. At the time every businessman in the country was against it. When it went to the Senate, which was a Conservative Senate, it was killed. If there was anything the Senate of Canada ever did to justify its existence it was the killing of the bill for the construction of a railway into the Yukon Territory. Then there was a great howl, among people with whom I have been affiliated for years, against the Senate. That died out in a few years' time and the businessmen of this country impressed upon the government of the day the inequity of building a road into the Yukon Territory.
There comes to my mind another occasion in 1912. Sir Robert Borden came into power in 1911. Sir Wilfrid Laurier's government had a plan to build a navy in this country under the control of the Dominion of Canada. When Sir Robert Borden came into power something had to be done, in the opinion of his government, and a bill was introduced in the House of Commons for the purpose of giving to Great Britain a tremendous lot of money to build naval ships. These naval ships were to be built in the old land and were to be controlled by the British Admiralty. That matter was discussed in this house without anybody having a wink of sleep from twelve o'clock on a Monday until twelve o'clock the following Saturday. During that debate the rules of closure were brought into the house. Finally the bill was passed in the house and it went to the Senate. At that time there happened to be a Liberal Senate and they turned down the bill. In my opinion that was the second time that the Senate of Canada justified its existence. There was quite a howl for a year or so from our Conservative friends on the matter of Senate reform.
I rather agree with the gentleman who spoke a while ago. I think charity should begin at home, and that we should do something about reforming this very house along certain lines, and that is something over which we have jurisdiction. But at the same time, as I said a moment ago, if there is any way of doing anything to the Senate that will make for better government in this country for the whole of Canada, then I am in favour

of it. But I do not think I have heard anything in the speeches so far that would convince me that it is necessary to reform the Senate along certain lines.
First of all, in regard to reforming the Senate, there has to be an amendment to the British North America Act before it can be done. We may pass all the resolutions we like in this house; we may say we are going in for reform of the Senate, but unless the Senate agrees, there is no constitutional power which will make them agree to anything that we do in this house, and that is proper.
The British North America Act contains the constitution of this country; it contains the constitution under which the Senate is organized in this country. Until the British North America Act is amended, or there is some understanding between the various provinces, the House of Commons and the Senate, it is useless to talk about Senate reform.
I do not like to hear people say anything derogatory about the Senate. I do not think anything derogatory was said about senators as such, but I have heard it said in the past. So far as calibre of governing and intellect are concerned, the calibre of the Senate from 1867 down to the present time compares very favourably with the membership in this House of Commons. It is true that Usually men a little older are sent to the Senate than most members who come into the House of Commons; but some years ago a very good rule was adopted. I do not think it is a rule, but it has become a custom that persons shall not be appointed to the Senate after they have passed their sixtieth birthday. Having regard to the death rate in this country in the past, few of them survive after their seventy-fifth birthday. Therefore, unless the life expectancy of people in this country is greatly extended, it is hardly necessary to insist that senators should get out when they reach seventy-five because they will not be there.
As I said, I am against the idea that we should do away with the Senate. As an institution it is something of which we should be proud. It is an institution that has done great work in this country. Since I came to the house the last time the thing that has struck me forcibly is that there has been a great reform in the Senate itself. I was in this house from 1911 on, 1917, 1921 and 1925. Rarely in those days was anything initiated in the Senate. I had not followed events from 1925 up until a year ago. I noticed that in this parliament a great deal of important legislation has had its initiation in the Senate, and when it comes to this house and goes into committee we can look back on the records

of the Senate committees and find out exactly what happened there, and it materially helps the work of this house.
Coming back again to the calibre of the Senate, I do not know whether I can point to people in this house who have any more ability to govern this country down through the years-I mean from the comparative standpoint-than the members who occupy Senate seats. I suppose that in this house we have men, including myself, of very poor calibre. We occasionally do have men who perhaps are not fully qualified in the matter of government. The same thing happens in the Senate-and that is not anything against the Senate.
Another point in favour of the Senate is that appointments are made to that body first because of business ability and secondly because they have had a good deal to do with government before their appointment to that body. Let me say-and I am not looking for a senatorship; if one were offered to me tomorrow I would not accept it-that I think it has been a good principle followed by both of the major parties to pick for seats in the Senate those who have had experience in government on the floor of the House of Commons. That is all to the good, so far as the Senate is concerned.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that I have completed all I wish to say.
I was paired with the right hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner). Had I voted, I would have voted for the amendment.
I was paired with the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Macdonald). Had I voted, I would have voted for the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, what I have to say perhaps might have been better said on motions when the

Manitoba Flood
Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made his statement on the flood situation, but I am almost certain that I would have been out of order. Therefore I have deferred making any statement until now. I want to tell those who are interested of those things which I actually saw, of those things of which I have firsthand information, but above all of thole things which I have felt, which I have lived through having worked with people who today are suffering in desolation and helplessness.
When I came to this country nineteen years ago I landed at the port of Halifax. _ The immigration officer who examined my goods and effects asked me for what city I was bound and I said, "Winnipeg." He said, "I am glad to hear that because I have just come from there. I have spent some of the happiest years of my life in that city and I have a great affection for it." That is an affection which I myself have found growing over the years. But today there is something more than affection, there is admiration for a city and for a people which ties me to them with bonds that cannot be broken. I have seen heroism, not the heroism of a sudden deed of derring-do or the heroism of some act of gallantry which leaves one almost aghast, but the heroism of people who were down and never knew what it was to be out, the heroism of people who, when they could scarcely lift another limb, nevertheless found within themselves the physical and spiritual strength to fight the encroachment of the river.
I am going to speak of Winnipeg not because I wish to slight any other area, far from it, but because I know what happened there. I am quite sure that what I say of Winnipeg and its people can be applied to every other area which has been afflicted by floods. Therefore the house will understand why I limit my remarks. Yet I know of the case of a farmer, a man near Ste. Agathe, who finally was compelled to surrender to the river, who at the last moment took his wife and children out in a truck leaving behind him about 8,000 bushels of grain, some 200 hogs which even then were strung along the wires squealing madly, leaving his horses and livestock, the last sounds in his ears being the screaming of animals which were doomed to almost certain death. I think of the little poultry rancher near St. Boniface whose whole livelihood was bound up with 1,700 chickens some seven weeks old, not ready for market. Knowing he could not rescue them he slaughtered them. Being a good citizen and knowing the responsibility he might incur by leaving
fMr. Stewart (Winnipeg North).]
dead poultry lying about and the corruption that might take place, not only did he slaughter them but he also burned them. I think of the market gardeners who have lost everything they had. These things I know only by hearsay but I know them to be correct.
When I landed in Winnipeg it was perhaps natural that I should go to the area where I stay. I found there what I knew of course, that for the second time in two years my wife and I were evacuated. At the worst, however, we find it only somewhat of a nuisance, and certainly only a nuisance compared with the losses which so many others have suffered. What struck Winnipeg was no turbulent flood leaving disaster in its wake such as we saw in the Fraser river valley, but a slow seeping flow of water which it appeared could not be dammed back. It was so slow that the water seemed to have the viscosity of oil and yet it was ruthless and indeed at times, almost frightening in its determination to conquer the city. That is the type of water which prevails of course in so many parts of the flooded areas.
As to the river itself, I have heard estimates that the current was only some seven or eight miles an hour. Yet I know on one occasion when I was out in a dinghy powered with a 12 horsepower outboard motor we were going against the stream and we made scarcely one mile an hour. It is a river with tortuous twists and bends, and being in flood naturally it has taken the shortest course to reach its destination and has swept straight across many sections of the city.
I think the time when our people suffered worst was over two weeks ago when rain started on Friday and continued. Altogether some two inches of rain, snow and sleet fell. It was during those days that heroism really was shown. Men and women would work for as long as seventy-two hours at a stretch without any respite in order to keep the river back. A friend of mine, for instance, the mayor of East Kildonan, who was the Progressive Conservative candidate in the last election, rose on Friday morning at seven o'clock and never saw his bed again until three o'clock on Tuesday morning. That experience was shared by many others, men and women alike.
The same story can be told of what happened in St. Boniface and on the dikes in Norwood. Working on the dikes, before lights were strung along them, was a most

Manitoba Flood
precarious and hazardous task. In some cases the dikes were 14 to 16 feet high and as much as 20 feet deep. Sandbags had to be lugged up the dikes over slippery, slithery, greasy mud. Nobody will ever know how people did not lose their lives by falling into the river which was but 6 inches below the top of the dikes on the other side. It is true some fell in but they were saved. The task of building the dikes almost staggers the imagination. I worked on them in four-hour shifts, and I know the physical condition I was in at the end of four hours. What then must have been the physical condition of those who worked not for hours but for days?
I saw the ramp which the city engineering department built up to the Provencher bridge to maintain communications between St. Boniface and the city of Winnipeg. Not hundreds but thousands of trucks of gravel were carried to this area and dumped there so that a road could be made through the flood. I saw boys and girls working on the dikes. I saw grandfathers and grandmothers working on them, and every age in between. There were nuns who were filling sandbags and building up dikes to save hospitals. I saw one man who was pointed out to me as the best safecracker in western Canada. He was out on bail and was spending every available moment and all his energy in helping to build dikes. Those who were fighting were citizens of all types from professional gamblers to preachers.
Of course there were incidents which struck one forcibly. I remember a case where a truck careened onto a sidewalk and stalled there. It took the people who were there twenty minutes to slap, pummell, and shake the driver of the truck into consciousness. When he came around it was learned that he had been forty-nine hours driving trucks of gravel to the Provencher ramp without any respite. There were other incidents which perhaps had a more humorous aspect, and people were very ready to see the humorous side of things. For instance there was the report which came over the radio station that all mothers and children should evacuate immediately but single girls and able-bodied men should stay behind. Fortunately many people saw the humour of that. Another case, perhaps not so humorous, is that of the man who saw three dead hogs floating near his house. He was determined that he would get rid of them. He tried the best he could but one slipped away from him and unfortunately crashed through the window of his living room, and so far as I know it is still there.
On the chesterfield.

As I say I
cannot speak of all parts of the city. Nevertheless I think my knowledge of what happened to one area will give members an idea of the situation. In Elmwood there was a tremendous fight to save the community. Men and women were working on the dikes day and night. They had to be sustained and canteens were set up by the women in homes, stores, community clubs, wherever it could be done, and hot food was taken to those who were working. Eventually it was organized on almost a professional basis. At first neighbours would go around trying to borrow a dozen eggs, some bacon or other meat, or anything which they could use to cook a hot meal. Women who were preparing their Sunday roasts would carve them up, place the dinner on a plate and send it down to the men who were working. EvAitually some two or three thousand meals a day were being served to those who manned the dikes, and all these meals were being cooked in the homes of the people. When I think of meals I must mention the valiant task which the Red Cross and the Salvation Army performed in every neighbourhood. Their work is beyond all praise. Men would be toiling and slaving on the dikes; along would come a truck from the Red Cross with some girls in it serving sandwiches, coffee and cigarettes. Similar aid, of course, was given by the Salvation Army. There were fishermen who came down from Gimli and the little island of Hecla up north in lake Winnipeg. They took their boats over to the mainland, loaded them on trucks and brought them down to help the beleaguered city. Farmers from Dauphin brought their trucks to help. I saw businessmen from Saskatoon who had nothing to offer but their labour; nevertheless they came to give what they had. I think one of the most impressive sights of all was a Canadian who had been evacuated once before from British Columbia because his skin was yellow. He was of Japanese origin; and in gratitude for the treatment he had received in Winnipeg he left his job and devoted all his time, day and night, to working on the dikes. He said he was glad to do it, because in that community he had been regarded as a human being. There was one difference between this man and other citizens. It was not the pigmentation of his skin. The difference lay in the fact that he had only one hand, having lost his right hand in an accident some two or three years ago.
But the danger is not yet past. It is all very well to read these Canadian Press reports saying that the danger is subsiding. Such is

Manitoba Flood
not necessarily the case. The river is only inching down, and there is still the possibility that dikes may go. But care is being taken to see that no lives are lost. In the Luxton area, for instance, which was visited by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), people can go to their flooded homes only when they get permission, when they get a boat, and when they have registered. They are given a card and go about their task, whatever it is; then on their return they surrender that card. In that way the community knows that no one will be lost.
At the same time, however, I think it is right to say that people are now getting their second wind. There is a growing feeling of security amongst them. The pressing urgency is subsiding; and now people are beginning to ask questions. Who is going to pay for the farm homes which have been destroyed? Who is goinf to pay for the livestock that has been drowned? Who is going to pay for the tractors and other implements that have been left to the mercy of the floods? Who is going to pay for those city homes which are so irretrievably damaged? Today the Prime Minister said that according to Central Mortgage and Housing there were some eight thousand of those homes. I think that is an understatement. The city of Winnipeg knows perhaps more about it than Central Mortgage and Housing, and their estimate is much higher. What of the man I saw with his wife; a man of about fifty-five, who throughout his working life had toiled to own his own home and who is now without work and also without a home? What about the veteran who placed all that he had in the way of rehabilitation credits in a home, which now has been devastated by the floods? The problem which faces Winnipeg and the surrounding community now is not so much one of relief as a tremendous social problem. We were confronted with this fact, for instance, that there are men out of work due to the floods. There were those who had lost their jobs, but whose families were still resident in the city. There were those who had lost their jobs, whose families had been evacuated, but whose homes were still intact. There were those who not only had lost their jobs and whose families had been evacuated, but who had completely lost their homes.
In the packing house industry, of which I know something, the members of the union across Canada decided they would raise money to maintain the incomes of those who had lost their jobs. We took up the matter with the big three packers, and eventually the packing house companies decided that as

a matter of policy they would pay all their men for time lost because of floods. That means the money which the union is now collecting can go into the general Manitoba relief fund. But I am sorry I cannot say the same practice is being followed by other branches of industry.
The question in the minds of the people is who is going to pay for all the damages. Obviously the municipalities cannot. Equally obviously the provincial government cannot. While we in Winnipeg and southern Manitoba are eternally grateful for the assistance that has come from every part of Canada, nevertheless it is clear that this fund which the Prime Minister seems to think will deal adequately with rehabilitation in the long run will amount to nothing more than a pittance. We had the extraordinary situation some weeks ago of the governments of Ontario and Saskatchewan offering all the assistance they could give and the premier of Manitoba, still blind to the menace confronting us, declining it. In Winnipeg the Prime Minister said that what he saw was a calamity. I think perhaps he used the wrong word; what he saw was a disaster. The calamity lay in the quality of leadership, or lack of leadership, given by the provincial authorities.
No one knows yet what is going to happen. The city of Winnipeg, by and large, is bearing the financial brunt not only for itself but for the surrounding municipalities. I live in the municipality of West Kildonan. There they could not afford to put down even one sandbag and the homes went by default. Yet the provincial government has done nothing to help this or other municipalities. Instead, the city of Winnipeg is today borrowing well over $100,000 a day, I am sure, for immediate flood purposes. This cannot go on indefinitely, yet still there is no word from any senior government, whether it be provincial or federal, as to what help will be given.
It is eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I therefore move the adjournment of this debate.

PREMIER'S OFFICE Saskatchewan
Regina, April 15, 1950
The Right Honourable Louis S. St. Laurent,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Ontario.
My dear Prime Minister:
Thank you for your letter of March 13th, in which I note you request some expansion of Item 6 ("Education") of the topics the government of Saskatchewan thought should be placed on the agenda of the Dominion-Provincial Conference to be held this autumn.
In brief, it is our feeling that there should be a minimum standard of educational opportunity available to all the children of Canada. It should make no difference whether the children are educated in the maritimes, in the central provinces or in the west. A high level of educational opportunity is basic to our democratic way of life.
However, great inequality of educational opportunity exists among the various provinces due to

Dominion-Provincial Conference
such factors as the number of children to be educated, distribution of population and financial ability of the province. The federal government is the only agency able to bring about an equitable distribution of educational opportunities. It is suggested, therefore, that this problem should be recognized by the federal government, and that rectifying steps be taken either by considering educational need as a factor in determining the amount of federal subsidy, or as a problem warranting special and direct financial assistance from the federal government. It is further suggested that such financial assistance does not in any way need to interfere with provincial jurisdiction in the field of education.
I am sure that you would agree that the future of our nation is dependent upon the children of today. The standard of their education should not be determined by locality. We feel confident that this problem can only be adequately dealt with on a nation-wide scale. In our opinion the provision of assistance to establish a minimum standard of education could be accomplished by federal grants to education without any interference with the exclusive jurisdiction over the matter of education which is now enjoyed by the provinces.
For these reasons, we feel that this subject should be given serious consideration by the conference.
Yours sincerely,
T. C. Douglas
